title: From Russian athletes to Iranian hackers: EU weighs tougher action
content:
EU foreign ministers called for Russian athletes to be kept out of sporting events in the bloc and for tighter visa policies on Monday. The Brussels meeting also addressed cyberattacks on French supermarket freezers, with further sanctions against Iran now being prepared.

Ministers made “a strong call to tighten visa policies and to prevent Russian athletes from competing in sports events that are held in the European Union”, EU foreign-policy chief Kaja Kallas said after the meeting. She did not announce an EU-wide ban or explain how the restrictions would be implemented.

The call accompanied new sanctions against Russian financial and energy interests, preparations for further measures against Moscow and additional equipment to help Ukraine through the winter.

Ms Kallas said the EU was mobilising 500 generators and 200 buses for Ukraine, alongside emergency shelters, underwater energy cables and floating bridges. EU leaders will discuss Ukraine’s financing needs for 2027 at their meeting on 26–27 November.

title: Rwanda could become Europe’s destination for rejected asylum seekers
content:
Austria, Germany, Denmark, Greece and the Netherlands are exploring a scheme that could send rejected asylum seekers to the African country, aiming for transfers in 2027.

The Austrian government announced the talks on Monday at a Vienna press conference with Chancellor Christian Stocker and Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen. The centre would receive people who cannot return to their home countries. Negotiations are to begin immediately, but a final agreement has yet to be concluded.

“We have been working on this for years,” Danish Immigration and Integration Minister Morten Bødskov said. He called for a system that prevents people from profiting from vulnerable migrants and stops abuses of European hospitality.

The scheme would apply to people who have exhausted their legal options to remain in the participating countries. Unlike Britain’s abandoned Rwanda plan, it would not cover people whose asylum applications are still in processing. The five governments had announced in September that they were working towards an arrangement with a country outside the EU.
snippet: Austria, Germany, Denmark, Greece and the Netherlands are exploring a scheme that could send rejected asylum seekers to the African country, aiming for transfers in 2027.
creator: Klára Odstrčilová

title: 113 more targets: How is the EU tightening the screws on Russia?
content:
Russian banks, oil networks and online retail are among the latest targets as Brussels seeks to choke off the money sustaining Moscow’s war machine. Foreign-policy chief Kaja Kallas accused the Kremlin of using peace talks to prolong the fighting.

Speaking before the Foreign Affairs Council in Brussels, Ms Kallas said Russia was repeating demands made before its full-scale invasion and adding further conditions. “This is also a clear pretext for keeping the war going,” she said in her arrival remarks. She urged negotiators to secure a ceasefire before moving to broader discussions.

The new sanctions cover 12 individuals and 101 entities, including nearly 50 Russian banks and financial institutions. “The EU is cutting off the financial channels that process state revenues and fund Russia’s war effort,” the Council said.

The sanctions also reach Russia’s online retail sector, targeting the sole shareholder of Wildberries and an individual controlling a majority stake in Ozon. Energy-sector listings include businesses operating Russian refineries and the St Petersburg oil terminal, alongside companies involved in oil exploration and production.

title: Two weeks to get home. Estonia shuts its Russian border
content:
Estonia is shutting every road into Russia. The crossings close on 1 December, after a foiled arson attack on a drone factory that Tallinn blames on Russian military intelligence. In Narva, families split by the river have two weeks left to visit relatives.

The target was Threod Systems in Viimsi, a company that builds reconnaissance and attack drones for Ukraine. Shortly after 3 a.m. on Saturday, the attackers smashed its windows and poured flammable liquid inside. They wanted an explosion and a fire. They got neither. The firm’s guards and the police reached them in time. The Internal Security Service (Kapo) detained eight suspects, all living in neighbouring Latvia.

Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna announced the closure on Sunday evening, citing “clear evidence” that Russia’s GRU military intelligence ordered the attack. Prime Minister Kristen Michal called the plot part of Russia’s hybrid war against Europe. It is not the first. In August, arsonists struck Milrem Robotics, a Tallinn company that makes ground robots for Ukraine.

title: Brussels clears the way for Europe’s biggest bank deal since the global financial crisis
content:
A €45bn landmark cross-border takeover marks a new test for Europe’s fragmented banking market.

The European Commission on Monday unconditionally approved UniCredit’s planned takeover of Germany’s Commerzbank. Brussels found that the €45bn deal would not harm competition on the German banking market. For UniCredit, that removes a major regulatory hurdle — and brings Europe closer to its biggest cross-border banking deal since the global financial crisis.

UniCredit completed its offer for Commerzbank shares in July, taking its stake in the German bank to 48 per cent. By the end of the year, it wants to secure roughly half of Commerzbank’s voting rights and effectively take control.

Under EU rules, major mergers and acquisitions must pass the European Commission’s competition test. Brussels must assess whether a deal would significantly restrict competition in the European Economic Area.

In the case of UniCredit and Commerzbank, the Commission focused mainly on Germany’s banking market. The two banks overlap across almost every major area of banking. UniCredit operates in Germany through HypoVereinsbank.
snippet: A €45bn landmark cross-border takeover marks a new test for Europe’s fragmented banking market.
creator: Anna Marvanová

title: Why do Europe’s best defence ideas end up in the US?
content:
A small European company builds a military prototype with EU money. Then it hits a wall of testing, certification, and procurement that can take years. European lawmakers now want to knock that wall down.

The road from prototype to the armed forces can take years, and investors are hard to find along the way. By the time a product reaches the market, military requirements may already have changed. This is one of the problems facing Europe’s defence industry, according to a report the European Parliament adopted on Thursday by 411 votes to 133, with 41 abstentions.

MEPs warn that small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) and start-ups developing defence technologies struggle to turn innovation into operational capabilities. As a result, some promising companies cannot scale up, while others look for investors outside Europe.

Lawmakers identify two critical bottlenecks, which they call ‘valleys of death’. The first separates the development of a technology from its military validation. The second comes after successful testing, when companies still have to find customers willing to buy and deploy their products.

title: Stuck on repeat. How AI recommendations sideline Europe’s artists
content:
Your feed picks the next song. ChatGPT picks the next book. Your streaming service already knows your next series. But the AI behind this easy discovery keeps pushing what is already popular. European artists warn that newcomers and minority-language voices are getting lost.

AI recommendations increasingly shape what we read, watch, and listen to. These systems use data about our preferences, behaviour, or even other users’ interests to suggest what we might enjoy next. But the way they decide what deserves our attention is still very opaque. European artists warn that AI recommendations make the fight for attention harder, particularly for emerging artists.

A recent European Commission study connected the availability and visibility of European cultural works to opaque recommendation algorithms, language barriers, and digital platforms’ tendency to amplify mainstream content. Similarly, a study examining book recommendations in Danish public libraries found that authors from less popular nationalities received up to 40 per cent less exposure.

title: A home of your own? Elusive dream as property prices outpace incomes
content:
The gap between what Europeans earn and what it costs to buy a flat or a house is widening, fuelling a crisis that threatens to spill beyond the housing market.

In Spain, frustration over unaffordable housing erupted this week into one of the biggest protests in recent years. Around four million workers took part in a nationwide general strike, according to trade unions. It was the first of its kind in 14 years. Thousands took to the streets of Madrid, Barcelona and other cities.

Most demonstrations remained peaceful, but clashes with police broke out in some places later in the evening. Rubbish bins were set alight and protesters threw objects at officers.

Spain faces a particularly acute shortage. According to the country’s central bank, it lacks around 750,000 homes. Meanwhile, rising rents are putting growing pressure on households priced out of homeownership.

title: Ukraine’s drone war never belonged to Fedorov, says defence entrepreneur
content:
Most wounded soldiers on Ukraine’s front lines are now hit by drones. Fedir Serdiuk, co-founder of defence company MOWA, tells EU Perspectives that Ukraine is ready to join Europe’s defence market. What it lacks are practical ways in.

EU Perspectives first spoke to Mr Serdiuk in April about what the EU can learn from Ukraine’s battlefields. Much has changed since. In July, President Volodymyr Zelensky dismissed Defence Minister Mykhailo Fedorov, and in August Ukraine’s parliament appointed Yevhen Khmara in his place.

We spoke again shortly before the Abu Dhabi peace talks of 10–11 November. For Brussels, his message is clear. “Ukraine is absolutely ready to be integrated with EU defence market and defence space but now it’s a U-turn to find practical and measurable tracks to integrate both industrial-wise.”

It’s been four and a half years since the large-scale invasion by Russia started, and it’s for me every day is a gift. Because it’s the formidable power and very serious military power that Russia presents. Also very brutal and capable, unfortunately, with a lot of resources. So being able to defend as good as we are doing this is itself a very good, a very good scenario.
snippet: Most wounded soldiers on Ukraine’s front lines are now hit by drones. Fedir Serdiuk, co-founder of defence company MOWA, tells EU Perspectives that Ukraine is ready to join Europe’s defence market.
creator: Federica Tessari

title: ‘Promise without money protects noone.’ Climate-hit health systems get a third of what they need
content:
A new global alliance launched at COP31 will bring together climate and health research funders, as countries face pressure to turn promises into action.

Forty-eight developing countries say they need $3.3bn (approx. €3.0bn) a year to prepare their health systems for climate change. In 2024, international finance covered less than 34 per cent of those needs, according to the 2026 Lancet Countdown report. At the UN climate summit in Antalya (COP31), the EU’s new health pledge is aimed at research.

On 13 November, the European Commission launched the Multilateral Initiative on Climate & Health Research Funding with the Wellcome Trust and public research funders from five continents. The Commission calls it the first global alliance of funders dedicated to climate and health research.

The pressure in Antalya is to deliver, not to promise. “COP31 must be the COP of implementation,” says Brazil’s Health Minister Alexandre Padilha, whose country hosted last year’s summit. “More than making political commitments, we need to turn them into concrete actions.”
snippet: A new global alliance launched at COP31 will bring together climate and health research funders, as countries face pressure to turn promises into action.
creator: Nicole Verbeeck

title: ‘Europe cannot compete at yesterday’s speed’: Pharma industry wants reform, patients demand a say
content:
From clinical trials moving to China to growing concerns over medicine supply chains, Europe’s pharmaceutical sector is facing mounting pressure to become more competitive. The EU’s proposed Biotech Act aims to reverse the trend. But industry and patient groups disagree on the price of making Europe an innovation hub.

The proposed European Biotech Act is intended to strengthen Europe’s position in global pharmaceutical research and development, support innovation, and encourage companies to keep their investments in the EU. Yet a roundtable in the European Parliament revealed differing views on how far the EU should go to attract industry investment and who should benefit from the resulting incentives.

If we have all the active substances manufactured in China, what is the first step they will take in case of any conflict? They will stop it. And then we have no chance to bring medicines to European patients.
— David Kolář, President, AIFP

title: We need ‘Friends of Global Europe’: Foreign policy expert on EU’s budget blind spot
content:
When EU governments sit down to negotiate the budget, farm and regional funding have plenty of defenders. Money for the bloc’s work around the world is easier to cut, says development policy expert Alexei Jones. He argues that the EU wants greater influence on the world stage but is unwilling to put money behind that ambition.

The Irish presidency’s latest proposal would cut the Global Europe heading by €33.064 billion, or 17.4 per cent, compared with the European Commission’s original proposal for the 2028–2034 budget (MFF). The instrument funds both development cooperation and projects that advance the EU’s strategic interests.

While cuts to agriculture and cohesion funding spark widespread political controversy, reducing the spending on external action remains relatively undisputed. That is not only remarkable, but also inconsistent with the EU’s wider calls for strategic autonomy and sustainable partnerships, argues Dr Alexei Jones of the European Centre for Development Policy Management (ECDPM). He tells EU Perspectives why the EU needs to rethink the role of its external budget in achieving those goals.

title: Faster trials, less red tape. If Europe doesn’t act, patients could miss out on new treatments
content:
Europe risks losing further ground to the US and China in clinical research unless it makes trials faster and easier to run. But improving regulatory timelines will need to go hand in hand with investment in hospitals, better coordination and stronger patient involvement.

The proposed European Biotech Act offers an opportunity to address some of the barriers facing clinical trials in the EU, from fragmented approval procedures to administrative burdens. But participants of a roundtable in the European Parliament cautioned that shortening deadlines on paper will not automatically translate into faster access to innovative treatments.

“Clinical trials are a fundamental part of pharmaceutical innovation. They are essential not only for developing new treatments, but also for ensuring that European patients can participate in research and benefit from medical advances,” said MEP Ondřej Krutílek (ECR/CZE), who hosted the discussion together with the Czech Association of the Innovative Pharmaceutical Industry (AIFP).
